title: Discretely-Refined Multi-view Clustering via Aligned Anchor Learning
one_liner: When clustering large datasets across multiple views, feeding discrete cluster assignments back into the graph refines which samples matter most.
lead: Multi-view clustering groups samples using information from multiple data sources at once. Anchor-based methods speed this up by working with a few representative samples rather than all samples. But existing methods split the work into two separate steps: building the consensus graph and assigning clusters, which means the continuous embeddings (the learned number-lists) and discrete cluster labels (the actual cluster IDs) never talk to each other. DRMC fixes this by continuously feeding discrete assignments back into graph refinement, forcing the two to align.

problem.h2: Clustering stumbles when graph-building and label-assigning ignore each other
paras: A typical approach to grouping samples from multiple data views works like this: build a similarity graph from the anchor samples (a tiny representative subset), then find clusters in that graph. These two steps are separate — the algorithm tweaks the graph in one phase and assigns clusters in the next, never letting them influence each other. The trouble: when the graph is built, it does not know which clusters will be assigned. When clusters are assigned, they do not flow back to reshape the graph. This one-way street means you lose information about which groupings the graph actually supports.

A beginner might try: improve each step independently, hoping better graphs lead to better clusters. This fails because the graph and cluster labels are two sides of one coin — when you ignore their connection, you leave the whole system stuck in a local dead-end where the graph supports the wrong clusters and nothing forces it to change.

callout.html: DRMC feeds discrete cluster assignments back into graph construction, making graph and clusters refine each other until they align.

steps.text: Select a small set of representative samples; build similarity graphs across all data views.
From anchor-to-anchor similarities, infer how similar each full sample is to every other, broadening the signal.

steps.b: Learn embeddings and assign clusters jointly.
steps.text: Run spectral embedding (extracting number-lists from the graph structure that place similar samples close) and cluster assignment at the same time, not separately.
Use orthogonal alignment (rotating the embedding number-lists to match the cluster label structure exactly).

steps.b: Feed labels back to refine the graph.
steps.text: Use the discrete cluster assignments to reshape the consensus graph; repeat until convergence (the numbers stop changing).

paras: The paper modifies the consensus graph — the single unified similarity graph built from all data views. Instead of building it once and using it to assign clusters, DRMC reshapes the consensus graph in light of the discrete cluster labels, so the graph evolves to support the clustering it discovers.

hidden.h2: Alignment quality between embeddings and cluster labels
hidden.name: embedding-label alignment
paras: Alignment measures how much the continuous embeddings (the learned number-lists from the graph) agree with the discrete cluster assignments (which samples are marked as belonging to the same cluster). A perfect alignment means when you read off the cluster label for a sample and look at its embedding numbers, they point to the same group. A poor alignment means the embeddings and labels contradict — a sample's numbers look close to one cluster while its label says another.

The paper estimates this alignment by rotating the embedding matrix (via orthogonal transformation, a kind of rigid turn that preserves distances) to maximize overlap with the discrete indicator matrix (a structure that marks which samples share labels). If the rotation is tight, the embeddings and labels were already in sync; if a large rotation is needed, they were pulling apart.

heat.caption: Darker means better embedding-label alignment. Refinement cycle helps (row 9) because feeding labels back reshapes the graph. When dark, embeddings and cluster labels point to the same groups.

reads.html: The alignment is the degree to which the learned embeddings and the assigned cluster labels agree on which samples should be grouped together. Better alignment means the algorithm has found a consistent story across both representations, because when embeddings and labels point to the same clusters, the graph, the learned numbers, and the assigned labels all reinforce one another instead of pulling apart.
The paper measures alignment via rotation of the embedding matrix to match the discrete indicator matrix, comparing the distance before and after rotation.

mechanism.h2: How discrete feedback refines the graph
paras: The core insight: a consensus graph is only useful if it supports the clusters you want. Normally, you build the graph once, then discover clusters in it. But if the graph does not naturally support clean clusters, you are stuck — the graph was built without knowing what clusters should look like.

DRMC breaks this bind by running graph construction and clustering in a loop. Each iteration, the algorithm assigns discrete cluster labels. Then, before building the next graph, it asks: given these cluster labels, which links in the graph are redundant (samples in the same cluster should already be close), and which links hurt (samples in different clusters should be farther apart)? It reshapes the consensus graph by strengthening within-cluster links and weakening between-cluster links. Then it learns new embeddings from this refined graph and assigns new labels. The discrete labels continuously feed back into graph structure, and the graph evolves to support the clustering it must explain.

This creates alignment: when embeddings and labels are misaligned, the graph-refinement step pulls them together. When they are aligned, the loop stabilizes because discrete labels and refined graph now agree.

stages.s: Learn embeddings and assign clusters jointly
Measure alignment between embeddings and labels
Reshape consensus graph using cluster feedback
Check if labels changed; if yes, loop back

math.words: The method minimizes a loss that balances three goals: spectral embedding consistency (embeddings should place similar samples close), discrete clustering (assigning clear cluster labels), and alignment penalty (embeddings and cluster labels should point to the same clusters). The alignment is enforced via orthogonal rotation of embeddings to match the discrete indicator matrix.
math.equation: L = L_embed + L_cluster + L_align; L_align = ||Z - Z^* || where Z^* is Z rotated to maximize overlap with indicator matrix C
symbols: loss for learning embeddings from the graph
loss for assigning discrete cluster labels
loss for aligning embeddings with cluster labels
the embedding matrix (rows are samples, columns are learned numbers)
the rotated embedding that best matches cluster structure
the discrete indicator matrix (entry (i, j) = 1 if samples i and j are in same cluster, else 0)
distance (how far apart the two matrices are after rotation)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose 3 samples cluster into 2 groups: samples 1,2 in cluster A; sample 3 in cluster B.
Indicator matrix C marks this: C[1,2]=1, C[1,3]=0, C[2,3]=0 (same cluster or not).
Embedding Z initially places sample 1 at (0.8, 0.1), sample 2 at (0.6, 0.2), sample 3 at (0.1, 0.9).
Samples 1 and 2 are close (embeddings similar) but samples 1 and 3 are far (embeddings opposite) — already aligned!
Rotation trying to match C keeps samples 1,2 close and 1,3 far — no large rotation needed.
L_align is small, so the loop converges: embeddings and labels agree.

math.note: The alignment loss forces the embedding number-lists to reflect the cluster label structure; discrete feedback reshapes the graph to support that alignment.

items.html: If the anchors do not represent the diversity of the full dataset, the anchor graphs miss true structure. The sample-level similarities inferred from them will be thin, and discrete feedback will have poor material to refine. If the anchor set is too small or biased, the method cannot recover.

items.b: Embeddings and labels become trapped in disagreement.
items.html: If the joint learning phase assigns labels that the embeddings disagree with, and the graph refinement cannot resolve it (because the anchor graphs do not support that clustering), the loop may oscillate or converge to a poor local solution. Orthogonal alignment tries to fix this but cannot force agreement from thin signals.

If the different data views suggest incompatible groupings, the consensus graph tries to blend them. Discrete feedback then tries to refine the graph toward one unified clustering, but it may suppress valid structure from one view. The method finds A clustering, not necessarily the right one.

When anchors are diverse, views agree on main structure, and the joint learning can find a stable alignment, discrete feedback progressively refines the graph to support cleaner clustering, and embeddings and labels converge to mutual agreement.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small multi-view dataset: for example, synthetically create 3 views of 100 samples forming 5 clear clusters. Run DRMC over 10 iterations, logging the alignment loss (how far embeddings are from cluster label structure) and the clustering accuracy (fraction of samples assigned to correct clusters). Plot both quantities over iterations. The demo should show: (1) alignment loss shrinks toward zero as the loop refines the graph, (2) clustering accuracy rises and stabilizes, (3) without the discrete feedback loop (frozen graph after step 1), both metrics plateau early at worse values, proving the refinement loop is essential.
demo.metric_eq: alignment_loss_t = ||Z_t - Z_t_rotated|| where Z_t_rotated matches cluster indicator matrix at iteration t; clustering_accuracy = (samples assigned to correct cluster) / (total samples)
demo.closing: The key proof: turn off the discrete feedback loop (build the consensus graph once and never touch it). Alignment loss stops improving and clustering accuracy plateaus, because without feedback the graph stays frozen and cannot reshape itself to support better clusters. Turn the loop back on; both metrics improve until convergence, because discrete labels now reshape the graph and embeddings relearn based on the refined graph, pulling everything toward agreement. This proves discrete feedback drives the refinement.
